claims.text: A surrogate model using pre-characterized microstructural descriptors can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior of HfNbTiVAl10 with accuracy comparable to established full-scale simulations.
Reported HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure containing a matrix, nanoscale or microscale precipitates, and coherent interfaces.
Phase fractions, interfacial characteristics, misfit strain, and characteristic length scales are relevant inputs for physics-informed or machine-learning mechanical-property models.
Interfaces, precipitate distributions, and lattice distortions in the hierarchical heterostructure govern local load transfer and deformation mechanisms.
Quantitatively linking static microstructural descriptors to macroscopic responses can capture essential alloy-strengthening physics.
Lattice distortion and solid-solution effects influence strength and elastic modulus in high-entropy alloys.
Precipitate phase fraction and size can influence critical resolved shear stress and yield strength.
Static microstructural descriptors can account for the local stress distributions controlling crack initiation in HfNbTiVAl10.
The surrogate model will reduce the need for computationally intensive full-scale simulations.
The model will predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture parameters within ±5–10% of experimental measurements.
The model will reduce computation time by roughly one order of magnitude relative to conventional DFT, atomistic, or full finite-element simulations.
Established atomistic, DFT, and finite-element methods are accurate for the targeted elasticity, yield, and fracture predictions.
First-principles simulations of disordered multicomponent alloys are computationally challenging, and explicit DFT evaluation of fracture or yield strength is mostly out of reach.
The surrogate approach may fail when the hierarchical microstructure evolves through phase transformations or defect evolution during deformation.
The surrogate approach may fail when uncharacterized local heterogeneities dominate the mechanical response and static descriptors are insufficient.
Preliminary evidence suggests that the surrogate model can achieve the stated accuracy and efficiency gains.
Prediction error and computational savings may vary with microstructural complexity and testing conditions.
Prediction errors greater than ±10% for the measured properties will falsify the hypothesis.
A computation-time reduction below 50% relative to standard simulation methods will falsify the hypothesis.
